title: Find your break-even
principle: Break-even is the sales you need to pay your fixed costs.

screens.text: Lata sends out 50 tiffins a day. Her customers love the food, but every month she still loses money.

screens.prompt: Each tiffin leaves Lata ₹30. Rent and her cook cost ₹1,800 a day. How many tiffins pay for that?
screens.why: 60 tiffins × ₹30 = ₹1,800. At 50 a day she falls short.

screens.title: Break-even
screens.text: Break-even is the number of sales that pays your fixed costs. Below it, you lose money. Above it, you make a profit.

screens.title: Lata's sum
screens.text: Fixed costs ÷ margin on one sale = break-even. For Lata: ₹1,800 ÷ ₹30 = 60 tiffins a day.

screens.prompt: Lata's rent goes up. Now her fixed costs are ₹2,100 a day. Each tiffin still leaves ₹30. What is her new break-even?
screens.why: ₹2,100 ÷ ₹30 = 70. Higher fixed costs push break-even up.

wrong.a: 60 was the old number. Divide the new ₹2,100 by ₹30.
wrong.b: ₹2,100 is the cost in rupees. Divide it by the ₹30 margin.

screens.prompt: Fixed costs are ₹1,800 a day. Lata sells 50 tiffins at ₹30 margin. What happens?

wrong.b: ₹1,500 is her margin. Rent and the cook still take ₹1,800.

screens.prompt: Which of Lata's costs goes into her break-even sum as a fixed cost?

options.label: A steel box for each tiffin

screens.why: The cook is paid the same, busy or not. Rice and boxes are counted in the margin on each tiffin.

wrong.a: Rice grows with each tiffin. It is a variable cost.
wrong.c: Boxes grow with each tiffin. They are a variable cost.

screens.prompt: Lata raises her price by ₹10. Each tiffin now leaves ₹40. Fixed costs stay ₹1,800. Her new break-even?
screens.why: ₹1,800 ÷ ₹40 = 45. A bigger margin means fewer sales to break even.

wrong.c: 60 was with a ₹30 margin. The margin is now ₹40.

screens.prompt: Put the steps to find break-even in order.
steps: List rent, pay and other fixed costs
Divide the total by your margin on one sale
Check: do you sell that many?
screens.why: List the fixed costs, then add them. Divide by the margin. Last, compare with your real sales.

screens.setup: Your friend wants to open a juice stall. Rent and a helper will cost ₹1,200 a day. Each glass leaves ₹20. He hopes to sell 40 glasses a day.
screens.question: He asks what you think. What do you say?

options.label: "40 glasses at ₹20 gives you ₹800 a day."
options.outcome: He opens. He thinks he makes ₹800 a day. Really he loses ₹400 a day.
options.why: ₹800 is his margin. Rent and the helper still take ₹1,200.
options.better: Take fixed costs off first: he needs 60 glasses to break even.

options.label: "Open and see how it goes."
options.outcome: He sells 40 a day and loses ₹400 a day before he sees why.
options.why: Trying is good, but a two-minute sum would have shown the gap.

options.label: "You need 60 a day just to cover costs."
options.outcome: He watches the spot for three days and counts buyers. Then he opens, knowing his target.
options.why: ₹1,200 ÷ ₹20 = 60. At 40 a day he would lose ₹400 a day.

summary: Break-even = fixed costs ÷ margin on one sale.
Below break-even you lose money. Above it you profit.
Higher fixed costs push break-even up.

cards.front: Fixed costs: ₹1,000 a day. Each sale leaves ₹20. How many sales to break even?
Your rent goes up. Your margin stays the same. What happens to break-even?
cards.back: It goes up. You need more sales to pay the higher rent.
